finding.claim: SQL injection in /search: the user-supplied query parameter q is interpolated into an f-string SQL statement, letting an unauthenticated attacker break out of the LIKE string literal and run arbitrary read queries (e.g. UNION SELECT over sqlite_master or any table) against shop.db.
finding.source: app.py:11 — request.args.get("q", ""), an arbitrary HTTP query-string value supplied by any remote client with no authentication.
finding.sink: app.py:12 — db.execute(f"SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{term}%'"), raw string concatenation into SQL executed on the shared sqlite3 connection.

trace.note: term = request.args.get("q", "") — attacker-controlled input, no validation or length limit.
term is placed verbatim inside the single-quoted LIKE literal via f-string; a quote character closes the literal, and -- comments out the trailing '%'.
db.execute runs the resulting SQL; fetchall() returns all rows of the injected query.
jsonify(rows) returns the injected query's rows directly to the attacker, so the injection is readable (not blind).

finding.guards_checked: No parameter binding on line 12 (unlike lines 18 and 25, which use ? placeholders, so the developers knew the pattern). No escaping of quotes or LIKE wildcards. No input allowlist or length cap. No authentication or authorization on the route. No error suppression: a malformed payload produces an sqlite3 error, but that also confirms injectability. Multi-statement stacking is blocked by Python's sqlite3 execute(), so the practical impact is read access (UNION SELECT), not writes. Repro: GET /search?q=' UNION SELECT name, sql FROM sqlite_master --  (2 columns match the id,name projection).

verdict.guard_found: none. app.py:11 reads the raw query parameter; app.py:12 interpolates it into the SQL via an f-string with no parameter binding, escaping, or allowlist. The route at app.py:9-10 has no authentication or authorization decorator. Python's sqlite3 execute() rejects stacked statements, so the impact is read-only, as the candidate said. app.py:13 returns fetchall() results directly, so the injection is not blind.
verdict.reason: The line numbers and behavior in the trace match app.py:11-13: the unauthenticated /search route (app.py:9-10) takes q into an f-string SQL LIKE literal at app.py:12 and returns the rows via jsonify at app.py:13, with no effective guard, so the UNION-based read injection is reachable and readable. The one assumption is that this app is deployed with the /search route exposed to untrusted clients.

finding.claim: No authorization on the owner-scoped listing: /by-owner returns every product for any owner string the caller supplies, with no check that the caller is that owner. If product ownership is meant to be private, any unauthenticated user can enumerate the catalogue of any owner.
finding.source: app.py:24 — request.args.get("owner", ""), an attacker-chosen value from the query string.
finding.sink: app.py:25-26 — SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE owner = ? returned to the caller via jsonify.

trace.note: owner taken directly from the query string; there is no session, token, or identity check anywhere in the file.
parameterized query, so the owner value cannot inject SQL, but it also selects by an attacker-chosen key.
Full result set returned to the caller.

finding.guards_checked: The query is parameterized (no SQLi here). The file contains no auth decorator, middleware, or ownership check, and no config or other modules exist in the repository that could add one. Confidence is lower because the intended audience of owner-scoped listings is not documented. Whether this is a vulnerability depends on whether the owner field is meant to be private.

verdict.guard_found: none. app.py:22-26 has no auth decorator, session, token, or ownership check. The only other file is app.py itself, so no middleware or config exists. The query at app.py:25 is parameterized, which blocks SQL injection but not this access-control issue.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: app.py:24 takes `owner` from the query string, app.py:25 filters on it with no identity check, and app.py:26 returns all matching rows to an anonymous caller. Whether this is a vulnerability depends on whether product ownership is meant to be private, which the code does not state, so severity is conditional even though the missing check is confirmed.

finding.claim: /product/<pid> exposes any product by sequential integer id without authentication. This is probably intended for a public shop, but the id is enumerable and the response includes price, so it is also the sole source of price data for every product.
finding.source: app.py:17 — pid, the integer path parameter, supplied by the caller and converted to int by Flask.
finding.sink: app.py:18-19 — parameterized SELECT id, name, price; response via jsonify(row).

trace.note: jsonify(row): a tuple becomes a JSON array; None becomes null with status 200 for missing ids.

finding.guards_checked: Parameterized query and int converter prevent injection. No auth, which is consistent with a public catalogue. Included as low-severity, for documentation of intent. Drop if public product data is intended.

verdict.guard_found: none. The int converter (app.py:16) and parameterized query (app.py:18) prevent injection but are not access controls. No auth check, decorator, or ownership filter exists on the route (app.py:16-19).
verdict.reason: All trace lines match the code: the route at app.py:16 takes any integer, the lookup at app.py:18 is parameterized, and app.py:19 returns jsonify(row), which yields null with status 200 for a missing id. An anonymous caller can enumerate every product's price, so the claim holds, but it is low severity and only a finding if the catalogue is meant to be private, as the candidate itself notes.

finding.claim: /search has no LIMIT and no minimum query length, so a single request with q=% (or an empty q) returns every product row. Combined with the LIKE wildcard behaviour, this allows cheap, repeated full-table scans and large responses.
finding.source: app.py:11 — q, attacker-controlled; empty default at line 11.
finding.sink: app.py:12-13 — unbounded fetchall() and jsonify(rows) on the full products table.

trace.note: q defaults to empty string and is not length-limited.
LIKE '%%%' or LIKE '%%' matches every row; fetchall() loads the full result.
entire result serialised into one JSON response.

finding.guards_checked: No LIMIT, pagination, rate limit, or request-size cap anywhere in the file. Severity is low for a small catalogue; it becomes relevant at scale or with the SQL injection above, which can also return unbounded data.

verdict.guard_found: none. app.py:11 reads q with a "" default and no length check. app.py:12 runs an f-string LIKE query with no LIMIT, and fetchall() loads every match. app.py:13 serialises the whole result with jsonify. There is no auth decorator, rate limit, or pagination anywhere in app.py.
verdict.reason: The route at app.py:9-13 is anonymous, and no control at app.py:11-13 caps the result set, so a request with q="%" or an empty q returns every row of products in one response. The claim is accurate but low severity: the impact depends on table size, and the same lines contain a more serious SQL injection at app.py:12 that should be reported as the primary finding.
